\chapter{Where, and When}
\label{ch:mr-where-when}
\hlchaptermodality{38}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask where somebody lives and when they are coming, and I can turn any statement I already own into a question by swapping one word and moving nothing.}

Complete MR-R38-where-when and ask three questions about one person -- who, where, when -- then tell the two question types apart by whether the voice has to rise.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[kuṭhe]{\mr{कुठे} (kuṭhe) — where}

\label{lesson:MR-C38-kuthe}



\begin{quote}
Two chapters ago you learned to add one more thing with \textbf{\mr{सुद्धा}}. Last chapter gave you \textbf{\mr{कोण}} and \textbf{\mr{किती}}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{koṇ}, then \emph{kitī}, then \emph{sudhā} in one breath
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{कुठे}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{कुठे}} — \emph{kuṭhe} — \textbf{where}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{तुम्ही} \mr{कुठे} \mr{राहता}?} — \emph{tumhī kuṭhe rāhtā?} — \textbf{where do you live?}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मी} \mr{पुण्यात} \mr{राहतो}.} — \emph{mī puṇyāt rāhto.} — \textbf{I live in Pune.}
\end{quote}

That exchange is the second question of almost every spoken interview, and until this lesson the book could write the answer and not the question. You already had \textbf{\mr{पुण्यात}} — the city with \textbf{-\mr{ात}} glued on its tail. What was missing was the word that asks for it.

\textbf{\mr{कुठे}} is the \textbf{\mr{क}-} family again, from Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{कुत्र}} (\emph{kutra}, \textquotedblleft{}where\textquotedblright{}). Its answer is a place, the way \textbf{\mr{कोण}} wants a person and \textbf{\mr{किती}} wants a number.

When you do not know: \textbf{\mr{माहीत} \mr{नाही}} — \emph{māhīt nāhī} — \textbf{I don't know}. That is a complete and polite answer to \textbf{\mr{कुठे}}.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kuṭhe} — where
  \item \emph{tumhī kuṭhe rāhtā?}
  \item \emph{māhīt nāhī} — the answer when you do not know
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What shape of answer does \textbf{\mr{कुठे}} want? (\textbf{A place}.) Which form field on your A1 profile answers it? (\textbf{\mr{शहर}}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%95\%E0\%A5\%81\%E0\%A4\%A0\%E0\%A5\%87}{Wiktionary: \mr{कुठे}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kadhī]{\mr{कधी} (kadhī) — when}

\label{lesson:MR-C38-kadhi}



\begin{quote}
You can already put two events in order with \textbf{\mr{जेव्हा} … \mr{तेव्हा} …} and with \textbf{-\mr{ल्यावर}}. Both of them ANSWER a question you cannot yet ask.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say a \emph{jevhā … tevhā …} sentence, then the same idea with \textbf{-\mr{ल्यावर}}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{कधी}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{कधी}} — \emph{kadhī} — \textbf{when}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{तुम्ही} \mr{कधी} \mr{येता}?} — \emph{tumhī kadhī yetā?} — \textbf{when are you coming?}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{उद्या}.} — \emph{udyā.} — \textbf{tomorrow.}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\mr{कधी}} is Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{कदा}} (\emph{kadā}, \textquotedblleft{}when\textquotedblright{}), and it is the fourth \textbf{\mr{क}-} word in four lessons. The family is now large enough to be a rule rather than a coincidence: \textbf{\mr{काय}}, \textbf{\mr{कोण}}, \textbf{\mr{किती}}, \textbf{\mr{कुठे}}, \textbf{\mr{कधी}}.

Notice where it sits. A Marathi time word comes early, before the verb — you saw that with \textbf{\mr{उद्या} \mr{भेटू}}. \textbf{\mr{कधी}} takes exactly that slot, because it is standing in for the answer.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kadhī} — when
  \item \emph{tumhī kadhī yetā?}
  \item \emph{koṇ}, \emph{kuṭhe}, \emph{kadhī} — person, place, time
  \item \emph{nako} — the word that refuses an offer, so you can decline as well as answer
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where in the sentence does a Marathi time word go? (\textbf{Early, before the verb}.) So where does \textbf{\mr{कधी}} go? (\textbf{The same place}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%95\%E0\%A4\%A7\%E0\%A5\%80}{Wiktionary: \mr{कधी}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[… kuṭhe …?]{Where the asking word stands}

\label{lesson:MR-C38-wh-order}



\begin{quote}
You have said \textbf{\mr{तुमचं} \mr{नाव} \mr{काय} \mr{आहे}?} and \textbf{\mr{तुम्ही} \mr{कसे} \mr{आहात}?} for many chapters. Both are questions. Neither one told you the rule they obey.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: nothing moves to the front}]
English hauls its asking word to the front of the sentence: \emph{your name is Aruṇ} becomes \emph{what is your name}. Marathi does not move anything. The asking word simply stands \textbf{in the slot where the answer would stand}, and the verb stays last.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{तुमचं} \mr{नाव} \mr{अरुण} \mr{आहे}.} $\to$ \textbf{\mr{तुमचं} \mr{नाव} \mr{काय} \mr{आहे}?}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{तुम्ही} \mr{पुण्यात} \mr{राहता}.} $\to$ \textbf{\mr{तुम्ही} \mr{कुठे} \mr{राहता}?}
\end{quote}

Read those two pairs across. In each, exactly one word changed and nothing else moved. That is the whole rule, and it is worth having as a rule rather than as two memorised phrases: it means every asking word you own works in every sentence you own, without rearrangement.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} a statement, then the same sentence with \textbf{\mr{कुठे}} in the answer's slot
  \item \emph{Say it:} the same trick with \textbf{\mr{कधी}}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{kitī} and put it where a number would have gone
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does a Marathi asking word stand? (\textbf{In the answer's own slot}.) What moves to the front? (\textbf{Nothing}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kuṭhe? · kadhī?]{Two ways to ask, and how to tell them apart}

\label{lesson:MR-R38-where-when}



\begin{quote}
Marathi now gives you two kinds of question. One ends in \textbf{\mr{का}} and is answered \textbf{\mr{हो}} or \textbf{\mr{नाही}}. The other carries a \textbf{\mr{क}-} word and is answered with information.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{koṇ}, \emph{kitī}, \emph{kuṭhe}, \emph{kadhī} — the four you now own, in order
  \item \emph{Say it:} one \textbf{\mr{का}} question, with the voice rising at the end
  \item \emph{Say it:} one \textbf{\mr{कुठे}} question, with the voice NOT rising — it does not have to
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{kāy}, the oldest of the family, and the sentence you have used it in since chapter nine
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which kind of question needs the rise, and which does not? (\textbf{The \mr{का} question needs it; a \mr{क}- question already shows itself in a word}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
